title: Pointer Types and Sizes
concept: Pointers interpret data differently depending on the type they point to

steps.title: Including stdio.h Header
steps.explanation: Header for using ```printf```. ```sizeof``` is a **compile-time operator**, not a function, so it doesn't need a separate header — but ```stdio.h``` is needed to print its result.

steps.title: Starting the main Function
steps.explanation:
The program starts — ```main```'s **stack frame** is created on the stack. Four variables will be created inside: ```a```, ```c```, ```pi```, ```pc```.

Key question: ```int*``` and ```char*``` point to targets of different sizes (4 bytes vs 1 byte). Are the pointers themselves different sizes too?

steps.title: Declaring Variables
steps.explanation:
`int a = 10` and `char c = 'A'` prepare values of different types.

These two have different sizes and interpretation methods, serving as reference data to explain the difference in pointer types.

steps.title: Declaring Pointers
steps.explanation:
`pi` stores `a`'s address, `pc` stores `c`'s address.

Both variables are pointers that hold addresses, but the size and interpretation method when dereferencing differs based on the type (`int*`/`char*`).

steps.title: Size of an int Pointer
steps.explanation:
`sizeof(pi)` gives the size of the pointer variable itself, not the target it points to.

Pointer size depends on the system architecture — on 64-bit systems, it's typically 8 bytes.

steps.title: Size of a char Pointer
steps.explanation:
`sizeof(pc)` is the same as `sizeof(pi)` on the same system.

This means pointer size is determined by the architecture's address size, not the target type.
steps.stdout:
Size of int*:  8
Size of char*: 8

steps.title: Reading a Value via int Pointer
steps.explanation:
`*pi` reads the data at that address as an integer (following `int*` rules) and gets the value 10.

The pointer type determines how data is interpreted when dereferencing.
steps.stdout:
Size of int*:  8
Size of char*: 8
Read int*:  10

steps.title: Reading a Value via char Pointer
steps.explanation:
`*pc` reads the data as a character (following `char*` rules) and gets `A`.

Even with the same address operation, different pointer types result in different read sizes and interpretations.
steps.stdout:
Size of int*:  8
Size of char*: 8
Read int*:  10
Read char*: A

steps.title: Program Termination
steps.explanation:
`return 0;` terminates the program and cleans up stack variables.

To summarize: pointer size depends on the environment, but the type determines the dereferencing interpretation rules.

quiz.question: On a 64-bit system, what is sizeof(p) for `double *p;`?
quiz.explanation: Regardless of whether the pointer points to a double or anything else, the pointer itself stores an 'address', so on a 64-bit system it's always 8 bytes.

misconceptions.correct:
No.
All pointer variables have the same size.
misconceptions.why: Only the size of the target they point to differs — the length of the address itself is the same.

keyTakeaway: All pointers are the same size, but the type acts as a map that determines 'how many bytes to read.'
